extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film fans, and film researchers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia entry summarizing the 2005 comedy film Wedding Crashers, covering plot, cast, production, release, critical response, home media, legacy, and box-office performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box office / commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: The film grossed $288.5 million worldwide on a $40 million budget; it was the 6th highest grossing film of 2005 in the United States and the first R-rated comedy to make $200 million at the domestic box office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures of commercial success highlighted include opening weekend gross ($33,900,720), domestic total (over $209 million), international gross, and relative ranking in the yearly box office. The page calls the film a 'sleeper hit' and notes studio expectations versus actual returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregated critical scores: Rotten Tomatoes approval rating 75% (185 reviews, average 6.6/10); Metacritic score 64/100 (39 critics); CinemaScore audience grade A−.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregator scores and audience polling as standard quantitative measures; also consider representative critics' quotes and qualitative takeaways (e.g., 'raunchy and sweet', praise for comic performances, or specific criticisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and on-screen chemistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting choices (pairing Vince Vaughn and Owen Wilson) and chemistry were central; casting of Claire involved auditioning over 200 actresses; disputes over casting Secretary Cleary (Walken vs. studio preferences) are noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes importance of lead pairing and chemistry to comedic effect, rapid casting decisions based on readings, and director/studio disagreements about casting tone. Casting unknown or international actors (Isla Fisher) and trusting test readings (Bradley Cooper) are cited as production decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers encouraged improvisation from the cast, especially Wilson and Vaughn, leaving breaks in the script for improvisation; Vaughn improvised for over 25 seconds in one scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing improvisation and leaving scripted gaps can generate extended comic beats and memorable moments; this is presented as a deliberate directorial/production choice to enhance comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Director David Dobkin insisted on three and a half weeks of rehearsals before filming, based on his theater background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant rehearsal time prior to shooting is highlighted as a production practice intended to prepare actors and refine performances for better on-screen comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of setting and location to serve comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The script was moved from Cape Cod to Washington, D.C.; Dobkin felt using his hometown would make location choices easier and that D.C. as a setting for a comedy would be unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting an unexpected or personally familiar setting can provide fresh comedic context and practical location advantages; location choice is tied to tone and production logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving rating to retain comedic content
rubrics_metrics.description: Dobkin considered releasing a non-R-rated version but abandoned the idea after realizing 'The two funniest scenes in the movie would have had to go.' Ultimately the R rating was kept to preserve key comedic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining an appropriate content rating can be crucial to preserving core comedic scenes; commercial considerations to broaden audience must be balanced against creative intent and funniest moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic staging and filming techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific scenes were staged/shot to feel authentic—e.g., the family football scene was shot in the manner of an NFL television broadcast to make it seem authentic and familiar to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using recognizable visual language or authentic production techniques can sell comedic set-pieces and heighten audience recognition (and therefore comedic effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining premise with emotional core
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers were initially doubtful the wedding-crashing premise could sustain a feature, so they added female love interests and an exploration of male friendship as the emotional core to make the story viable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To expand a high-concept premise into a feature film, embed an emotional throughline (e.g., friendship, love) and additional character stakes that give the plot durability beyond the gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social sensitivity and potential to age poorly
rubrics_metrics.description: Later reassessments criticized the film for dated or offensive elements: a date-rape joke, use of the 'sassy racist grandmother' trope, a predatory gay-man trope, trivialization of rape, and underdeveloped female characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that comedic choices (jokes, stereotypes, portrayals of gender/sexuality/violence) can age poorly and attract criticism; sensitivity and character development influence long-term critical reassessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home media strategy and alternate cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Home media releases included an unrated 'Uncorked Edition' with eight new minutes integrated into the film, audio commentaries, deleted scenes, featurettes, and a 'Rules of Wedding Crashing' text gallery; the film earned an estimated $145 million from home media sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementary materials and alternate cuts can extend a film's lifecycle and generate substantial additional revenue; including extras (commentary, deleted scenes, galleries) is a common home-media strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural impact / quotability
rubrics_metrics.description: The film produced memorable contributions to pop culture, e.g., the phrase 'stage-five clinger' entered the popular lexicon; Entertainment Weekly named it among the most quotable comedies since 1970.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term cultural impact (quotable lines, phrases entering common usage) is a non-quantitative measure of a comedy's legacy and influence.
